guidingQuestion: How do ecosystems change over time?
hook: Lava hardens into bare rock, a beaver plugs a stream, a prairie dog town goes quiet, and each change ripples out to many living things nearby, so how does a changed place stage its comeback?

objectives.text: Identify gradual and sudden changes to ecosystems, natural or caused by people, and describe how ecological succession rebuilds a community step by step on new or changed ground.

Explain how a change to a living part of an ecosystem (such as a prairie dog population) or a nonliving part (such as water flow, light or sediment) changes resources, raising some populations and lowering others.

objectives.text: Apply criteria and constraints to explain and evaluate designs that rebuild coastal wetlands, such as river diversions that deliver sediment while protecting nearby communities.

keyIdeas: Every ecosystem is a dynamic system. Its living and nonliving parts keep changing, sometimes slowly (a pond filling in, a glacier melting back) and sometimes suddenly (an eruption, a flood, an oil spill, a forest cleared by people).

Ecological succession is the slow replacement of one community by another. Hardy pioneers settle bare ground, build soil as they live and die, and make room for larger plants and more animals; a pond can become a marsh, a meadow and finally a forest.
Recovery after a big disturbance usually takes a long time, depends on survivors and new arrivals, and may rebuild an ecosystem like the old one or a different one.
Organisms are linked by resources, feeding relationships, shelter and other interactions, so changing one population, such as prairie dogs, can raise some populations and lower others.
Changing nonliving parts of an ecosystem, such as water depth and speed, light or sediment, changes which populations can thrive. Beaver dams change water depth, water speed and light.

Scientists build evidence by comparing many places with and without a species, or before and after a change, while keeping other conditions alike. A pattern shows what changed; an explanation proposes why.

Engineers restoring coastal wetlands define criteria (what success looks like) and constraints (limits such as cost and flood safety). The best design depends on local conditions, as the open Wax Lake channel and the gated diversion near New Orleans show.

glossary.definition: A system whose parts never stop changing, whether the changes are slow or fast, small or large. Every ecosystem is one.
The gradual, long-term replacement of one community of living things by another as conditions in a place change, such as a pond turning into a marsh, then a meadow, then a forest.
A hardy organism, such as a moss or small plant, that settles bare ground first and helps build soil for later arrivals.
Information gathered by observing or experimenting that can support, or argue against, an explanation.
All the members of one species living in the same area at the same time.
Something living things need from their surroundings, such as food, water, light, shelter or space.
An ecosystem where the ground is soaked with water much of the time, such as a marsh or a swamp.
A species that so many others depend on that losing it can shake up the whole ecosystem. Prairie dogs are one example.
A species that people have moved, on purpose or by accident, into an area outside its native range.
The standards used to judge whether a design solution succeeds.
Limits a design has to work within, such as cost, safety, materials or the space available.
Bits of sand, silt and mud carried along by moving water or wind and dropped somewhere else.
A raised, strengthened riverbank built to keep high water from spilling onto nearby land.
A channel or gated structure that sends part of a river's water, and the sediment it carries, in a new direction, such as into a bay or a wetland.

explorer.title: From Bare Ground to Forest
paragraphs: Every ecosystem is a dynamic system: its living and nonliving parts never stop changing. Some changes creep along, like a pond slowly filling with dead leaves or a glacier melting back. Others arrive all at once, like a lava flow, a hurricane, an oil spill or a forest bulldozed for a new road.

Ecological succession is the gradual replacement of one community by another. On bare ground, such as cooled lava or gravel left by a glacier, the first settlers are tough pioneers: small plants, mosses and tiny animals carried in by wind or by other animals. As they live and die they build soil, and that soil lets bigger plants and more animals move in.

A pond can follow a similar path. Dead matter piles up on the bottom until the pond becomes a marsh, then a meadow, and finally, as the soil deepens, a forest. Each stage changes the conditions, and the conditions decide which populations can thrive.

Recovery after a big disturbance, such as an eruption, is usually slow, often taking decades to thousands of years, and it is not guaranteed to rebuild the same ecosystem. Survivors left after a disturbance, such as roots, seeds and burrowing animals, can give recovery a head start.

diagram.caption: One common path of succession. Arrows point forward in time; they are not food links.
diagram.alt: A chain of four stages linked by arrows pointing forward in time: an open pond becomes a marsh or wetland as dead matter fills it; the marsh becomes a meadow as soil builds up; the meadow becomes a forest as the soil thickens. This is one common pattern of succession, and real places can follow other paths.

explorer.watchOut: Succession is a broad pattern, not a fixed timetable. The year labels on the textbook's pond-to-forest figure are illustrations, an eruption rarely kills absolutely everything, and a recovered ecosystem can end up different from the one that was there before.

explorer.title: One Change, Many Ripples
paragraphs: Organisms are tied together by food, shelter and other resources. Change one population and the effect travels along those ties, raising some populations and lowering others.

Prairie dogs show how far the ripples can reach. Their burrows shelter burrowing owls, rabbits and rattlesnakes. Their tunnels let water and air into the soil, and their clipping keeps grass short and fresh, so bison like to graze the nutritious regrowth on their towns. Black-footed ferrets eat almost nothing but prairie dogs. Where prairie dogs vanish, ferrets, burrowing owls and other burrow users tend to decline.

Not every species gains. Prairie dogs also clip back shrubs, so animals that rely on those shrubs can lose food. A species linked to this many others is sometimes called a keystone species: losing it can unsettle the whole ecosystem.

Nonliving changes ripple too. A beaver dam turns a fast stream into a deep, calm pond, lets sunlight reach the ground where trees were cut, and spreads water to plants far downstream. Pond animals, small plants, the moose and elk that eat them, and downstream plant communities all respond.

diagram.caption: Who tends to gain and who tends to lose when part of an ecosystem changes
diagram.alt: Table with four columns: change, part of the ecosystem changed, who tends to gain, who tends to lose. Row 1: more prairie dogs in a grassland changes a living part; burrowing owls, black-footed ferrets, rabbits and bison tend to gain; shrubs that prairie dogs clip back, and animals that rely on them, tend to lose. Row 2: a beaver dam floods a stream, changing a nonliving part, the water's depth and speed; pond plants and animals gain; species that need fast, shallow water lose habitat there. Row 3: beavers cut trees by the bank, letting in more light, a nonliving part; small plants and the moose and elk that eat them gain; the cut trees themselves lose.
rows: More prairie dogs in a grassland
Burrowing owls, black-footed ferrets, rabbits, bison
Shrubs that prairie dogs clip back, and animals that rely on them
A beaver dam floods a stream
Species that need fast, shallow water
Beavers cut trees along the bank
Nonliving: more light on the ground
Small plants; moose and elk that eat them

explorer.watchOut: Effects run in more than one direction, so don't label a change all good or all bad: prairie dogs clip back shrubs, yet grazers such as bison and pronghorn are drawn to the fresh regrowth on their towns. A beaver dam works mainly by changing nonliving conditions, even though beavers are alive.

explorer.title: Reading the Evidence
paragraphs: Scientists build evidence by comparing. They count species in many grasslands with prairie dogs and many without, or along streams with and without beaver dams, and look for patterns that repeat. One sighting could be chance; a pattern across many places is much stronger.
A fair comparison keeps other conditions alike. If the stream with a beaver pond also gets far more rain than the stream without one, the rain might explain its lush plants instead of the pond.

Before-and-after data show what changed. In the textbook's illustrated example of a Gulf of Mexico wetland altered by people, raccoons and cattle egrets increased; black bears, manatees and pocketbook mussels decreased; and blue catfish stayed about the same.
Keep the steps separate. An observation records what was measured, an explanation proposes why it happened, and a prediction says what should happen next so the explanation can be tested.

diagram.caption: A Gulf of Mexico wetland before and after people changed the landscape (relative sizes estimated from the textbook's illustrated graph; not real counts)
diagram.alt: Table of relative population sizes before and after people changed a Gulf of Mexico wetland, on a scale where 4 is the largest. American black bears: 1 before, 0 after. Manatees: 2 before, 0.5 after. Raccoons: 1 before, 4 after. Blue catfish: 2 before, 2 after. Pocketbook mussels: 4 before, 0 after. Cattle egrets: 0 before, 4 after.

explorer.watchOut: A before-and-after graph shows a pattern, not its cause. The textbook's Gulf graph is an illustration with no real counts, and its cattle egrets were not brought by people: they crossed from Africa to South America on their own and later spread across farmland.

explorer.title: Designing a Wetland Comeback
paragraphs: Louisiana's coastal wetlands were built largely from sediment that the Mississippi River carried to the coast. They give wildlife homes and food and soften storm surges before they reach towns. Levees and a rerouted Mississippi River now keep much of that sediment away from some of those marshes, and they have been shrinking.

Engineers start by defining criteria, the standards for success, such as healthy marsh and better storm protection, and constraints, the limits, such as cost and the rule that the project must not flood homes.

At Wax Lake, a channel dug in the early 1940s to ease flooding sends Atchafalaya River water and sediment into a shallow bay, and new delta land has kept forming there. Near New Orleans, a permanent opening could flood crowded neighborhoods, so a gated diversion in a levee lets river water into the marshes when it is safe and closes when high water threatens.
No single design fits every coastline. The best choice depends on local conditions, and engineers keep collecting data to check whether a design is really working.

diagram.caption: Two ways to send river water and sediment toward coastal wetlands
diagram.alt: Table comparing two designs. Wax Lake Outlet: a channel dug off the Atchafalaya River in the early 1940s that leads away from towns into a shallow, open bay; it was dug to lower flood levels for nearby towns; new delta land keeps forming. Gated diversion near New Orleans: gates built into a levee on crowded, low-lying land; the gates close when floods threaten; some marsh has regrown, and its main official goal is keeping salt water out of the marshes.
rows: Channel leads away from towns into a shallow, open bay
Channel dug off the Atchafalaya River in the early 1940s
Gates built into a levee on the Mississippi River
Dug to lower flood levels for nearby towns
Gates close when high water threatens
Some marsh regrowth; main official goal is keeping salt water out

explorer.watchOut: The textbook's Wax Lake map label says the channel joins the Mississippi River, but the Wax Lake Outlet carries Atchafalaya River water, and the 2.8 square kilometers per year figure describes two neighboring deltas together. The gated diversion near New Orleans was built mainly to hold back salt water, and how much land it builds is still debated.

reviewFlags.issue: OCR is empty or garbled on image-heavy pages: the p. 284 opener is a photo with no text; Figure 1 on p. 286 lost its 'Year 1500 / Forest ecosystem' panel; the p. 291 Key Science Concept graph lost every bar and has no numeric axis or color key; the NGSS box on p. 285 and the Figure 4 labels on p. 292 are letter-spaced or broken.
reviewFlags.resolution: All ten lesson pages were rendered and read. Figure 1 has four panels (Year 1 pond, Year 500 wetland, Year 1000 meadow, Year 1500 forest). The p. 291 graph was re-rendered at 250 dpi; bar heights were estimated in relative units, and the blue bars were read as 'before' and the gold bars as 'after' to match the blue-framed 'before' panel and the gold-framed 'after' panel. Questions L22-Q17 and L22-Q18 state that the values are relative estimates.

evidence.supports: The pond-to-forest figure shows four stages: pond, wetland, meadow and forest.

evidence.locator: Key Science Concept: Ecosystem Changes Shift Populations (rendered)
evidence.supports: The before-and-after graph shows black bears, manatees and pocketbook mussels falling, raccoons and cattle egrets rising, and blue catfish about the same.

reviewFlags.issue: p. 287 says an eruption can kill all living things in the area and completely wipe out an ecosystem. That is too absolute: after Mount St. Helens erupted in 1980, seeds, spores, roots, pocket gophers, fungi and ground-dwelling insects survived under the debris and helped recovery.
reviewFlags.resolution: The game says a large eruption can kill most living things nearby and that recovery draws on both survivors and new arrivals. L22-Q08 tests the role of survivors; the Explorer O1 card names it.

evidence.supports: Eruptions change ecosystems rapidly, and the area recovers slowly through succession.

evidence.title: Ecology - Mount St. Helens National Monument
evidence.supports: Seeds, spores, gophers, fungi, plants with underground buds and ground-dwelling insects survived the 1980 eruption and played a vital role in ecological recovery.

reviewFlags.issue: pp. 285-286 define ecological succession as 'predictable', and Figure 1 labels the stages Year 1, 500, 1000 and 1500. Succession follows broad patterns but not a fixed timetable or a guaranteed endpoint (p. 287 itself says the recovered ecosystem may differ).
reviewFlags.resolution: The game calls succession a common pattern, treats the figure's years as illustrations, and states that recovery is slow and not guaranteed to rebuild the same ecosystem (L22-Q03 conditions and limitations, L22-Q07, Explorer O1 watch-out).

evidence.supports: After recovery, the new ecosystem sometimes resembles the old one and sometimes differs.

evidence.title: Biology 2e, 45.6 Community Ecology
evidence.supports: Following a disturbance, a community may or may not return to its earlier equilibrium state; primary succession starts on newly exposed land with hardy pioneer species.

reviewFlags.issue: p. 289 says prairie dogs reduce flowering plants and shrubs, so pronghorn antelope decline. Other sources report the opposite: the National Park Service says changes in plant growth on prairie dog towns draw grazers such as bison and pronghorn, which benefit from the trimmed grass.
reviewFlags.resolution: Pronghorn are not used in any question. L22-Q14 keeps the textbook's general point (a change that helps some species can harm others) with an unnamed animal that depends on shrubs prairie dogs clip back, and its conditions state that the shrubs become scarce. The Explorer O2 watch-out names bison and pronghorn as grazers drawn to prairie dog towns. See also L22-RF10.

evidence.locator: Section 2, Some Species Do Not Benefit from Prairie Dogs
evidence.supports: Prairie dogs eat flowering plants and shrubs, leaving less of them for animals that eat those plants.

evidence.title: Prairie Dogs: Pipsqueaks of the Prairie
evidence.supports: Changes in plant growth on prairie dog towns bring grazers such as bison and pronghorn, which benefit from prairie dogs trimming the grass.

reviewFlags.issue: p. 288 says prairie dog numbers may have fallen to 2 percent of their level 100 years ago, a dated and uncertain estimate (the National Park Service gives a range shrunk to about 5 percent of its original size). The burrow illustration labels a 'jackrabbit' although the text says rabbits.
reviewFlags.resolution: No question tests the percentage or the rabbit species. The decline is described only as large, as estimated at the time the textbook was written.

evidence.locator: Section 2, Changes to Living Parts of Ecosystems
evidence.supports: Destroying grasslands for farming and other uses has greatly reduced prairie dog numbers.

evidence.title: Prairie Dogs: Pipsqueaks of the Prairie
evidence.supports: The original range of prairie dogs has shrunk to about 5 percent of its initial size, and black-footed ferrets eat prairie dogs exclusively.

reviewFlags.issue: The p. 291 spread says cattle egrets 'were introduced' after humans changed the Gulf landscape. Cattle egrets crossed from Africa to northeastern South America on their own in the 1870s-1880s and were unknown in North America before about 1952; their spread was helped by farmland and livestock, not by people releasing them. The graph is also a stylized illustration with no units or real counts.
reviewFlags.resolution: Questions describe cattle egrets only as absent before and common after. The Explorer O3 watch-out explains their natural arrival helped by farmland, and L22-Q17/Q18 call the values relative estimates from an illustration. The glossary defines an introduced species as one moved by people, on purpose or by accident (USDA NALT), so by the game's own definition the p. 291 cattle egrets are not introduced; the entry cites p. 287, not p. 291.

evidence.locator: Key Science Concept: Ecosystem Changes Shift Populations
evidence.supports: After people changed the Gulf landscape, some populations increased and others decreased; cattle egrets appear only after the changes.

evidence.title: Western Cattle-Egret, Guide to North American Birds
evidence.supports: Cattle egrets spread from Africa to northeastern South America in the 1870s and 1880s and were unknown in North America before 1952.

evidence.title: The Cattle Egret: The Opportunist
evidence.supports: Cattle egrets reached the New World on their own with little direct human help; the spread of rangeland, livestock and modern farming aided them.

evidence.title: introduced species (NAL Thesaurus concept)
evidence.supports: Introduced species are species brought by humans, intentionally or unintentionally, into a new geographic area outside their native range.

reviewFlags.issue: p. 292: the Figure 4 label says the channel was dug 'between the Mississippi River and the Gulf of Mexico', but the text (and NASA) say the Wax Lake Outlet carries Atchafalaya River water. The '2.8 square kilometers per year' rate matches NASA's estimate for the Atchafalaya and Wax Lake deltas together; NASA gives about 1.2 for Wax Lake alone, and growth varies with floods and hurricanes.
reviewFlags.resolution: The game names the Atchafalaya River. L22-Q26 presents 2.8 km² per year as one scientific estimate of the two deltas' combined rate (an LSU estimate reported by NASA) and states that real growth varies; the Explorer O4 watch-out names the label error.

evidence.supports: A channel dug in the early 1940s diverted Atchafalaya River water, and new wetlands formed as sediment was deposited.

evidence.title: New Land on the Louisiana Coast
evidence.supports: One estimate by Louisiana State University scientists, reported by NASA, says the Atchafalaya and Wax Lake Outlet deltas have combined to grow about 2.8 square kilometers per year; the Wax Lake delta alone grows about 1.2. The page does not say the estimate came from satellite studies.

evidence.title: World of Change: Growing Deltas in Atchafalaya Bay
evidence.supports: The Army Corps opened the Wax Lake Outlet in 1941 to reduce flooding in Morgan City; growth has varied with major floods and hurricanes; reeds and willows colonize the higher sandbars.

reviewFlags.issue: pp. 292-293 present the Caernarvon diversion as a project to rebuild wetlands that protect New Orleans and say wetlands have started to form again. Louisiana's coastal agency states its goal is to reduce saltwater intrusion and keep an estuarine gradient in Breton Sound, with marsh growth, less marsh loss and fish and wildlife productivity as objectives; it was built 1988-1991, and how much land it builds is debated.
reviewFlags.resolution: L22-Q24 tests only the gate logic (open when flooding is not a risk, closed when it is), which the agency's record of closures for flood advisories supports. The Explorer O4 card states the main official goal and that land-building results are debated. No question claims a specific amount of new land at Caernarvon.

evidence.locator: Section 4, Protecting Local Communities from Flooding
evidence.supports: A gated diversion built into a levee opens when there is no flood risk and closes when there is one.

evidence.title: 2024 Caernarvon Freshwater Diversion Operations and Monitoring Summary
evidence.publisher: Louisiana Coastal Protection and Restoration Authority (CPRA)
evidence.supports: Caernarvon is five gated culverts built by the Corps of Engineers between 1988 and 1991; its goal is reducing saltwater intrusion in the Breton Sound Basin; in 2024 it was closed 107 days for low river stage, National Weather Service advisories and saltwater intrusion.

reviewFlags.issue: The lesson describes first settlers on bare ground (pp. 285, 287) and a species whose loss destabilizes a whole ecosystem (p. 289) without naming 'pioneer species' or 'keystone species'.
reviewFlags.resolution: Both terms were added to the glossary with original, learner-facing definitions. This flag, not the glossary, records that the textbook describes these ideas without using the names. No question requires either term.

evidence.locator: Section 2, Prairie Dog Populations Change Prairie Ecosystems
evidence.supports: Prairie dogs are linked to so many species that the whole ecosystem's stability depends on them.

evidence.title: Biology 2e, 45.6 Community Ecology
evidence.supports: Hardy plants and lichens with few soil needs are pioneer species; a keystone species is key to maintaining biodiversity in an ecosystem.

evidence.title: Prairie Dogs: Pipsqueaks of the Prairie
evidence.supports: The National Park Service calls prairie dogs a keystone species that many other species depend on.

reviewFlags.issue: pp. 288-289 say prairie dog burrows make grass more abundant for bison and that prairie dogs reduce flowering plants and shrubs. The National Park Service pages the lesson cites describe something different: prairie dogs' constant clipping produces regrowth that is higher in nutritional quality, which draws bison and pronghorn, and clearing grass makes new space for forbs (flowering, broad-leaved plants). Neither page says colonies hold more grass. Grass is itself a flowering plant, so 'flowering plants and shrubs as well as grass' is loose wording. The shrub reduction is supported: in a five-year experiment, mesquite was three to five times more abundant where prairie dogs were removed.
reviewFlags.resolution: The game says burrows let water and air into the soil and help fresh grass grow, says bison favor the nutritious regrowth on prairie dog towns, limits the plants that lose out to shrubs, and never says prairie dogs make 'more grass' or cause 'fewer flowering plants' (L22-Q09, Q10, Q13, Q14, Q20, and the Explorer O2 card, table and watch-out). No claim is made about the total amount of grass on colonies, which the opened sources don't state.

evidence.locator: Section 2, Some Species Benefit from Prairie Dogs; Some Species Do Not Benefit from Prairie Dogs
evidence.supports: The textbook says burrows cause more grass growth that bison eat, and that growing prairie dog populations reduce flowering plants and shrubs by eating them.

evidence.title: Black-tailed Prairie Dogs
evidence.publisher: National Park Service (Scotts Bluff National Monument)
evidence.supports: Bison, bighorn sheep and pronghorn benefit from prairie dogs clipping the grass, because constant trimming produces growth that is higher in nutritional quality; prairie dogs probably clip vegetation to keep a clear view of approaching predators.

evidence.title: Prairie Dogs: Pipsqueaks of the Prairie
evidence.supports: Trimming by prairie dogs produces more nutritious growth that brings grazers such as bison and pronghorn to prairie dog towns, and clearing grass makes new space for plants such as forbs.

evidence.title: Interactive Effects of Black-Tailed Prairie Dogs and Cattle on Shrub Encroachment in a Desert Grassland Ecosystem
evidence.supports: Prairie dogs limit shrubs by clipping them and eating their seedlings; after five years, mesquite was three to five times more abundant in plots where prairie dogs were removed.
